patient.chief_complaint: Progressive confusion, unsteady gait, and low-grade fever over the past several days
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Soon-Ja Park is a 74-year-old right-handed Korean woman with a history of remote splenectomy for idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2, lumbar disc herniation, and previously diagnosed mild cognitive impairment who presents to the emergency department with progressive confusion and worsening gait instability over the past ten days, with new-onset low-grade fever over the past three days. According to her husband, the patient first began to show noticeable decline in her gait approximately five weeks ago, developing a shuffling, small-step pattern with frequent stumbles and near-falls. She was seen at an outpatient neurology clinic three weeks ago, where her gait abnormalities and worsening memory difficulties raised concern for possible normal pressure hydrocephalus given her age and clinical presentation. Brain imaging at that visit was noted to show ventricular enlargement, and further workup was planned. However, over the past ten days, her cognitive function has deteriorated more rapidly than expected. She has become increasingly confused, forgetting the names of family members, repeating questions, and on two occasions becoming disoriented in her own apartment. Five days ago, she developed a mild cough and nasal congestion. Her husband took her to a local primary care clinic three days ago, where she was diagnosed with an upper respiratory infection and started on oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. Despite the antibiotic treatment, she developed a low-grade fever two days ago, measured at 38.1 degrees Celsius at home. She began complaining of a diffuse headache that was not relieved by acetaminophen. Yesterday evening, she became notably more lethargic, had difficulty staying awake during dinner, and vomited once. Her husband also observed that she seemed to flinch and turn away from bright lights. This morning, she was difficult to rouse from sleep and could only state her name when questioned. Her husband called emergency services. In the emergency department, she intermittently opens her eyes to voice and follows simple commands inconsistently. She complains of neck pain when asked. The emergency physician notes her prior history of gait disturbance and cognitive decline and considers whether this represents progression of her suspected normal pressure hydrocephalus, but the acuity of the recent deterioration and new fever raise concern for an infectious process.

mri.impression: Communicating ventriculomegaly (Evans index 0.38) with crowded high-convexity sulci, initially raising consideration of normal pressure hydrocephalus. However, subtle patchy leptomeningeal enhancement in the basal cisterns and along the frontoparietal convexities raises concern for an infectious or inflammatory meningeal process, and may explain the hydrocephalus as secondary to impaired CSF reabsorption from meningeal disease. No evidence of cerebritis, abscess formation, or acute infarction. Chronic small vessel ischemic changes (Fazekas grade 2). Clinical correlation recommended.

differential_by_imaging.rationale: Leptomeningeal enhancement along basal cisterns and frontoparietal convexities with sulcal FLAIR hyperintensity and communicating hydrocephalus is a recognized imaging pattern of meningeal inflammation; enhancement distribution and hydrocephalus morphology favor an inflammatory or infectious meningeal process over primary CSF flow obstruction

Communicating ventriculomegaly with Evans index 0.38 and crowded convexity sulci is morphologically consistent with NPH; however, leptomeningeal enhancement is not a feature of idiopathic NPH and is atypical for this diagnosis
Leptomeningeal enhancement with communicating hydrocephalus can occur with meningeal carcinomatosis; imaging alone cannot exclude this entity

results.title: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis
results.authors: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, et al.
results.key_finding: Empiric therapy for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults >50 years: vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) plus ampicillin (for Listeria coverage). Adjunctive dexamethasone should be given before or with the first dose of antibiotics.

results.title: Pneumococcal meningitis in adults after introduction of PCV13
results.authors: Castelblanco RL, Lee M, Hasbun R
results.key_finding: Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in adults. Asplenic patients are at markedly increased risk due to impaired opsonization of encapsulated organisms. Case fatality rate remains 20-30%.

results.title: Duration of antibiotic therapy for pneumococcal meningitis
results.authors: Havens PL, Wendelberger KJ, Denver DR
results.key_finding: Recommended duration for pneumococcal meningitis is 10-14 days of IV antibiotics. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 4 days should be initiated before or with the first dose of antibiotics to reduce mortality and hearing loss.

output.summary: Empiric therapy for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults combines vancomycin with a third-generation cephalosporin; ampicillin is added for Listeria coverage in patients over 50 years or those with immunocompromise. Adjunctive dexamethasone has been shown in randomized controlled trials to reduce mortality and sensorineural hearing loss in bacterial meningitis, with greatest benefit in pneumococcal disease when administered before or with the first antibiotic dose. Treatment duration for pneumococcal meningitis is 10–14 days. Asplenic patients are at increased risk for invasive infections with encapsulated organisms and benefit from vaccination (pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal) at appropriate intervals.

sequence_constraints.reason: Per IDSA 2004, non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture whenever any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal neurological deficit, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60). LP performed in undetected mass effect can precipitate fatal herniation.

Blood cultures must be drawn (under interpret_labs) before the first dose of empiric antibiotics so that culture yield is not lost; in practice this means peripheral cultures are collected at the same draw as the CSF analysis is initiated, and the lab tube sequencing prevents antibiotic exposure before specimen acquisition.

critical_actions: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
key_reasoning_points: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Lower the index of suspicion for bacterial meningitis.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Gram-stain sensitivity is only 60-90% even untreated; multiplex PCR and antigen testing must be used to confirm the organism.

red_herrings.data_point: Communicating ventriculomegaly with gait and cognitive features resembling NPH

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The leptomeningeal enhancement and fever are not features of NPH; communicating hydrocephalus is a known complication of bacterial meningitis.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty: subacute presentation initially mimicking NPH, with partial antibiotic treatment confounding Gram stain results, asplenic patient at high risk for encapsulated organisms, and hydrocephalus creating diagnostic uncertainty between infectious vs idiopathic etiology. Key diagnostic clues require integrating CSF findings with clinical context rather than relying on a single pathognomonic test.
